    Tweezer Top

    A reversal pattern that forms after a rise when two consecutive candles reach almost the same high and the second one turns down. It can show that price failed to get past the same level twice and that sellers are waiting there.

    How it forms

    • There is a clear rise before it.
    • Candle 1 is usually green and continues the rise.
    • Candle 2 is red: it closes below its open.
    • The two candles' highs (wicks included) are almost the same; the difference is very small compared with the candles' size, for example a few percent of their range.

    The second candle tests the first candle's high but cannot get past it. The rule is about the highs; the size of the bodies is secondary.

    What it suggests

    The first candle shows buyers taking price to a new high. The second candle rises to the same high but is turned back there and closes lower. Failing to get past the same level twice can point to selling pressure at that price.

    The pattern is like a small double top made of two candles. On its own it does not prove the rise is over; how far down the second candle closes and where the pattern forms are read together.

    When it strengthens, when it weakens

    Strengthens

    • Forming at a resistance zone
    • Candle 2 closing below the middle of candle 1's body
    • A clear rise before it
    • High volume on candle 2
    • Forming on a higher timeframe (4H, 1D)

    Weakens

    • Forming in a sideways, directionless market
    • Candle 2 having a small body and closing just below the high
    • Very small candles
    • A strong support zone right below
    • Forming on very small timeframes

    The MarketLevelMap view

    How it relates to zones

    A tweezer top stands out most at a resistance zone. Both candles being turned back in the same zone can show that sellers are defending it. It reads as more meaningful when the common high is inside or just above the zone and the closes stay below it.

    The first support zone below the pattern shows how much room is left for a drop. If support is very close, the pattern is considered weaker.

    When it is invalidated

    If price closes above the common high (the highest point of the two candles), the bearish scenario is considered invalid.

    A candle that only wicks above the high and closes below it does not invalidate the pattern on its own.

    Often confused with

    • Tweezer BottomThe opposite: after a drop, two candles reach the same low and the second turns up.
    • Bearish EngulfingIn a bearish engulfing the red body covers the green body; in a tweezer what matters is the same high, not the bodies.
    • Double TopA double top is the same idea on a larger scale, made of many candles with a clear low in between.
